name: I Ching
info: The I Ching or Yijing, the Book of Changes, is an ancient Chinese divination text built on 64 hexagrams, later joined to the Ten Wings commentaries and made one of the Five Classics in the 2nd century BCE.

facts.made: A divination manual of the Western Zhou, traditionally ascribed to Fuxi, King Wen of Zhou, the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, an attribution no longer generally accepted; the Ten Wings commentaries are later and of unknown origin
facts.form: A text in Early Old Chinese of 64 hexagrams, each with a name, a hexagram statement and six line statements (two extra for hexagrams 1 and 2), bound with ten commentaries called the Ten Wings
facts.where: The oldest known manuscript, found in 1987, is held by the Shanghai Library; other early copies come from the Shanghai Museum's bamboo slips (found in 1994) and from Mawangdui (found in 1973); the official edition was cut in stone as one of the Xiping Stone Classics
facts.known: 64 hexagrams and 8 trigrams; the King Wen sequence; yarrow stalk and coin divination; the Ten Wings; one of the Five Classics; Leibniz's binary reading; Richard Wilhelm's 1923 German translation

t: The core of the book is the Zhou yi, a divination manual of the Western Zhou, which modern scholars date to between the 10th and 4th centuries BCE.
Over the Warring States and early imperial periods it gained the Ten Wings and became a cosmological text; in 136 BCE Emperor Wu of Han named it the first among the classics.
Commentators of many schools have read it for divination, moral guidance and philosophy, and it has been translated into Western languages dozens of times.
dyk: The Zuo Zhuan and Guoyu describe more than twenty divinations with the Zhou yi, made by professional soothsayers for royal families between 671 and 487 BCE, yet none of the stories uses a commentary or a stated method.
ev: last quarter of the 9th century BCE
Edward Shaughnessy dates the compilation of the Zhou yi in its current form to the early reign of King Xuan of Zhou
The Zuo Zhuan and Guoyu record more than twenty divinations using the Zhou yi for royal families
The Great Commentary, arguably the most important of the Ten Wings, is composed, and a Shanghai Museum copy shows the Zhou yi in use at all levels of society
Emperor Wu of Han names the Zhou yi the first among the classics and calls it the I Ching
Wang Bi writes his Annotated Book of Changes, which becomes the official commentary under the Tang
Zhu Xi reconstructs yarrow stalk divination from the Great Commentary, a method still in use
Leibniz writes the first European commentary on the I Ching
Richard Wilhelm's German translation appears; Cary Baynes's English version follows in 1950

sections.origins:
The core of the I Ching is a divination text of the Western Zhou dynasty called the Changes of Zhou (Zhou yi). Modern scholars suggest dates between the 10th and 4th centuries BCE for the assembly of the text in roughly its present form. The American sinologist Edward Shaughnessy, comparing its language with dated bronze inscriptions, dated its compilation to the last quarter of the 9th century BCE, in the early decades of the reign of King Xuan of Zhou (r. c. 827 to 782 BCE).

Tradition ascribed the work to the Zhou cultural heroes King Wen and the Duke of Zhou, and associated it with the legendary ruler Fuxi. Another tradition held that most of it was written by Tang of Shang. According to the Great Commentary, Fuxi observed the patterns of the world and made the eight trigrams. The Zhou yi itself says nothing about its origins. By the Han, a consensus formed around Ma Rong's attribution to Fuxi, King Wen, the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, but scholars no longer generally accept it.

It may not have stood alone: the Rites of Zhou names two other divination systems, the Lianshan and the Guicang.
sections.content:
The basic unit of the Zhou yi is the hexagram (gua), a figure of six stacked lines, each either broken or unbroken. The received text holds all 64 possible hexagrams. Each has a name, a short hexagram statement and six line statements. Hexagrams 1 and 2 have an extra line statement. The book opens with the words yuan heng li zhen, which recur in the hexagram statements and were already treated as important in the 6th century BCE. Shaughnessy reads them as an "initial receipt" of an offering, "beneficial" for further "divining".

Yin and yang are represented by broken and solid lines. Three lines make one of eight trigrams, and two trigrams combined make a hexagram. The line statements, which form most of the book, are exceedingly cryptic. They may give oracular or prognostic statements, and some contain poetry or references to historical events.

In the canonical text the hexagrams follow the King Wen sequence, named after King Wen of Zhou, who traditionally reformed the method of interpretation. The sequence generally pairs each hexagram with its upside-down equivalent. The numbering of hexagrams in binary or decimal is a modern invention.
sections.making:
The Zhou yi was written in Early Old Chinese. A copy among the Shanghai Museum's bamboo and wooden slips, discovered in 1994, shows it in use at all levels of society in its current form by 300 BCE, though small variations remained as late as the Warring States period. Another arrangement of the hexagrams, found at Mawangdui in 1973, groups them by shared upper trigram. The oldest known manuscript, found in 1987 and now in the Shanghai Library, was almost certainly in the King Wen sequence.

When the Zhou yi was canonised, it was bound to ten commentaries called the Ten Wings. They are of a much later date, written in a predecessor of Middle Chinese, and their specific origins remain a complete mystery to academics. The most important is arguably the Great Commentary (Xi ci or Dazhuan), dated to roughly 300 BCE. It describes the book as a microcosm of the universe and explains how the eight trigrams proceeded from the oneness of the universe through three bifurcations.

The Ten Wings were traditionally attributed to Confucius, possibly through a misreading of the Records of the Grand Historian. Evidence suggests he did not consider the Zhou yi a classic.
sections.reception:
In 136 BCE Emperor Wu of Han named the Zhou yi the first among the classics and called it the Classic of Changes, or I Ching. It joined the Five Classics, and the official edition was set in stone as one of the Xiping Stone Classics. It was not included in the burning of the Confucian classics. In the Eastern Han its interpreters split into two schools, one seeking symbolic and numerological parallels with nature, the other attending to the moral content. Wang Bi later discarded Han numerology, and under the Tang, Kong Yingda's Right Meaning of the Book of Changes, built on Wang Bi's commentary, became the standard edition through the Song.

By the 11th century the book was read as intricate philosophy. Cheng Yi read it as a guide to moral perfection. Zhu Xi, in the 12th century, argued that it was primarily a work of divination usable for moral self-cultivation. In 1557 the Korean philosopher Yi Hwang produced an influential study. In Edo Japan over 1,000 books on the I Ching were published by over 400 authors, and some early Edo writers ranked it the greatest of the Confucian classics.

The Kangxi Emperor was especially fond of the book and ordered new interpretations.
sections.survival:
The canonised I Ching was the standard text for over two thousand years, until alternate versions of the Zhou yi and related texts were found in the 20th century. Most early commentary, such as the image and number work of Jing Fang, Yu Fan and Xun Shuang, is no longer extant; only short fragments survive in a Tang dynasty text, the Zhou yi jijie. Over 150 editions of earlier Chinese commentaries were reprinted in Edo Japan, including several texts that had been lost in China.

Divination practice also came down in reconstructed form. The Great Commentary describes a process using a bundle of 50 yarrow stalks. Yarrow stalk divination dates to the Western Zhou, but its modern form is a reconstruction: Zhu Xi's version, still used across the Far East, and a rival reconstruction by Gao Heng. Coin divination became widely used in the Tang dynasty and remains in use, and dice and cards have appeared more recently.

Finds of the 20th century, among them the Mawangdui and Shanghai manuscripts, have let scholars study how the text was used before the Qin dynasty. Proponents of newly reconstructed Western Zhou readings, often very different from traditional ones, are sometimes called the modernist school.
sections.legacy:
The sinologist Michael Nylan describes the I Ching as the best-known Chinese book in the world. In East Asia it is a foundational text for the Confucian and Daoist traditions. The Japanese word for metaphysics, keijijogaku, derives from a statement in the Great Commentary, and the Yuan dynasty's official name, Da Yuan, was taken from the I Ching.

In Europe, Leibniz wrote the first commentary in 1703, arguing that the book showed the universality of binary numbers, while Hegel criticised the binary system and Chinese characters as "empty forms". The earliest complete Western translation was a Latin one by the Jesuit Jean-Baptiste Regis and his companions in the 1730s, published in Germany in the 1830s. James Legge and Thomas McClatchie translated it into English in the 19th century. Richard Wilhelm's 1923 German translation, put into English by Cary Baynes in 1950 with an introduction by Carl Jung, was historically the most influential.

The book had a notable impact on the 1960s counterculture and on figures such as John Cage, Jorge Luis Borges and Hermann Hesse. Pink Floyd's "Chapter 24" (1967) quotes the Wilhelm and Baynes text. Niels Bohr is credited with finding inspiration in yin and yang symbolism, while Joseph Needham argued that the book had impeded scientific development.

summary: The I Ching, or Book of Changes, began as a Western Zhou divination manual of 64 hexagrams. With the Ten Wings added, it became one of the Five Classics in 136 BCE, and it has been read for centuries as divination, moral guidance and philosophy across East Asia and, since the 18th century, in the West.

The article's lead says 500-200 BC for the Warring States and early imperial transformation; the Warring States period is elsewhere c. 475-221 BC.
